title: HICO: A Benchmark for Recognizing Human-Object Interactions in Images
limitations: HICO labels photographed human interactions with a bounded set of common object categories and is not a universal affordance inventory.
Co-occurrence frequency is a property of the sampled images, not evidence of artistic quality, desirability, or universal applicability.
The benchmark recognizes visible interaction categories but does not establish physical feasibility, task-specific grip, narrative role, weapon policy, or audience response.
Still-image labels can underdetermine action phase, causal direction, intent, and prior or subsequent object state.

title: Same Object, Different Grasps: Data and Semantic Knowledge for Task-Oriented Grasping
limitations: TaskGrasp uses a parallel-jaw robot gripper and household or kitchen objects, so its grasp geometry cannot be copied directly to human, animal, fantasy, or multi-limbed anatomy.
Object-task suitability and grasp labels include crowdsourced judgment and the paper reports annotation ambiguity; they are priors rather than physical guarantees.
The dataset does not cover the full range of tools, weapons, fictional props, scales, materials, or social meanings needed by illustration prompts.
Successful robot grasping does not establish visual legibility, narrative coherence, safety, cultural appropriateness, or aesthetic value.

research_questions: How can props remain concept-independent vocabulary candidates while their active affordances stay conditional on actor, task, target, embodiment, and scene?
How should an action-object relation be separated from the grip and contact geometry that realizes it in pixels?
How can uncommon or remote prop uses remain available without treating dataset frequency as quality or using creativity to bypass feasibility and policy?
Which typed fields keep an apple, hammer, and machine gun in one global pool while preserving their different physical, affective, violence, technology, and salience burdens?

mechanisms.statement: Represent an affordance candidate as a sense-specific action-object relation rather than attaching one timeless function to an object name.
Allow an object to retain several possible interactions while selecting only the interaction that participates in the current event spine.
Use semantic object and action relations to keep uncommon but coherent interactions retrievable without promoting sample frequency to a quality score.
Condition the visible grasp and protected contact region on the selected task because the same object can require materially different grasps for different uses.
Treat object-task used-for knowledge as a prior that still requires embodiment, scale, material, contact, target, and scene checks.
Resolve the action-object relation first, then jointly realize task-specific hand or body contact so a valid verb-noun label cannot float without physical evidence.
Keep apple, hammer, and machine gun as global candidates, but assign independent affordance, state, event-role, resource, distance, load, and guard fields instead of one universality flag.

Require a weapon candidate to carry typed state, target relation, event role, violence context, bystander exposure, and platform-policy status; creativity may rank policy-eligible candidates but cannot replace this gate.

candidate_definitions.uao_affordance_profile: A nonvisual object record containing candidate actions, required actor capabilities, target types, material and scale constraints, state requirements, and expected result types.
candidate_definitions.uao_action_object_pair: A sense-specific event relation binding one selected action to one prop participant instead of assigning an inherent universal function to the prop.
candidate_definitions.uao_cooccurring_affordance_set: A retained set of mutually compatible possible interactions for one object from which the event solver activates only the current role-bearing relation.
candidate_definitions.uao_task_conditioned_grasp: A visible hand, limb, mouth, tail, tool, or body contact configuration selected for the current task rather than reused across every use of the object.
candidate_definitions.uao_effective_contact_region: The object region that must remain accessible, unobscured, and unoccupied so the selected action can occur and be read.
candidate_definitions.uao_secondary_target_chain: A visible actor-to-prop-to-target chain used when the prop is an instrument acting on a second object or surface.
candidate_definitions.uao_global_prop_apple: A global edible-object candidate with generally low mass but variable offer, carry, inspect, cut, eat, symbolic, state, and affective roles; inclusion does not make it automatically suitable.
candidate_definitions.uao_global_prop_hammer: A global tool candidate whose carry, repair, construct, strike, inspect, or transfer use requires scale, grip, target, impact phase, material, and consequence checks.
candidate_definitions.uao_global_prop_machine_gun: A global weapon candidate with high violence, technology, physical-resource, and salience load that remains dormant unless typed state, target, event role, scene, bystander, and platform-policy gates pass.
candidate_definitions.uao_affordance_prior_guard: A guard that uses observed or researched action-object relations as soft retrieval priors and never as exhaustive allowlists or physical guarantees.
candidate_definitions.uao_frequency_quality_guard: A guard that prohibits converting dataset count, commonness, recognition accuracy, or annotation popularity into artistic quality, desirability, universality, or creativity.
candidate_definitions.uao_weapon_event_guard: A hard guard requiring weapon state, target relation, event role, violence context, bystander exposure, and platform-policy eligibility independently of creativity.

pixel_evidence_definitions.uao_task_conditioned_grasp: The selected hand or body contact visibly supports the declared task, with readable limb continuity and no contradictory grip on the same resource.
pixel_evidence_definitions.uao_effective_contact_region: The functional region used by the declared action remains visibly accessible and distinct from the gripping region when the task requires that separation.
pixel_evidence_definitions.uao_secondary_target_chain: Actor contact, prop orientation, second target contact or gap, and a compatible result cue form one readable directed chain.
pixel_evidence_definitions.uao_global_prop_apple: An apple is visibly bound to one event role such as held, offered, inspected, cut, eaten, stored, or transformed rather than placed as an unexplained decoration.
pixel_evidence_definitions.uao_global_prop_hammer: A hammer's head, handle, grip, target relation, action phase, and physical consequence or safe inactive state remain mutually readable.
pixel_evidence_definitions.uao_global_prop_machine_gun: A machine gun's high-level state, carrier relation, event role, target or explicit absence of a target, and scene context are visually separated from mere heroic display; pixel appearance never substitutes for policy review.

compatibility: An apple is compatible with low-load carrying, offering, eating, cutting, inspecting, storing, gifting, evidence, or symbolic roles when the event spine selects one.
A hammer is compatible with repair, construction, controlled impact, carrying, inspection, transfer, obstacle, or evidence roles when grip, target, scale, and consequence agree.
A machine gun may remain in the global vocabulary for storage, transport, surrender, inspection, guarding, historical display, or policy-eligible action when its typed weapon guard passes.
Task-conditioned grasp is compatible with non-hand embodiment only after the solver maps the same functional contact requirement to an available limb, mouth, tail, tentacle, mount, or tool.
One prop may expose multiple affordances internally, but the final still should show one primary event role and at most one compatible secondary relation.
A remote prop is compatible with a concept only when its action, role, state, and visible causal bridge return to the fixed identity core.
conflicts: A closed no-prop or empty-hand slot conflicts with every optional global prop regardless of creativity.
Two-handed operation conflicts with another simultaneous two-hand claim unless a support, mount, sling, assistant, release phase, or alternate embodiment resolves the resource conflict.
A hammer impact pose conflicts with no target, no swing clearance, an incompatible grip, or no readable contact or anticipated consequence.
A weapon candidate conflicts with absent weapon state, absent role, ambiguous target relation, unresolved bystander exposure, or failed platform-policy eligibility.
An affordance label conflicts with pixels that show only object presence and no actor, contact, target, phase, or result relation.
A dataset-common action conflicts with an explicit user prohibition even when it would otherwise rank highly.
counterexamples: An apple enlarged to dominate the frame can have higher salience and theme load than a small stored weapon, so object category alone does not determine load.
A ceremonial, toy, emergency, or repair hammer may not imply violence, while a small everyday object can become threatening through event role and context.
A machine gun secured in a museum display, transport case, or surrender scene may have a non-firing event role but still requires weapon and policy guards.
The same mug can be grasped differently for pouring, washing, handing over, or packing; one canonical grasp is not a universal affordance.
A rare action-object pair can be physically coherent and narratively useful, while a frequent pair can be dull, prohibited, or incompatible with the requested concept.
boundaries: Affordance data describes possible action relations and never grants permission, commands use, or establishes safety.
Do not provide detailed weapon-operation instructions or infer loaded status, intent, legality, or threat from appearance alone.
Platform safety and policy remain authoritative and cannot be replaced by creativity, semantic distance, rarity, or a local score.
Do not infer gender, age, disability, occupation, culture, personality, or morality from a chosen prop or grasp.
Do not treat one dataset's missing action-object pair as physically impossible or creatively invalid.
User-fixed props, actions, prohibitions, and closed slots outrank universal candidate retrieval.
domain_limits: HICO covers photographed people interacting with common objects and TaskGrasp covers robot grasps for household and kitchen tasks; neither spans all illustration domains.
Fictional magic, extreme scale, vehicles, mounted equipment, historical arms, medical devices, ritual items, and industrial machinery require separate domain knowledge.
Weapon, hazardous, medical, legal, and sexualized contexts require domain-specific policy and safety handling beyond affordance compatibility.
The matrix supports still-image event construction, not full motion planning or operational instruction.
embodiment_limits: HICO assumes visible human actors and TaskGrasp assumes a two-finger robot gripper; neither establishes direct compatibility for nonhuman anatomy.
Hands, mouths, beaks, paws, tails, tentacles, wings, mounts, prostheses, and tool-mediated contact require explicit capability and contact mappings.
Scale, reach, strength, joint range, support surface, balance, and limb occupancy must be resolved independently of semantic suitability.
Faceless or limbless subjects may participate through mounts, carriers, environmental mechanisms, assistants, or indirect consequences rather than fabricated human grips.
cultural_limits: Object functions, symbolic roles, acceptable handling, ceremonial meanings, and weapon readings vary by culture, period, community, and genre.
An apple, hammer, or firearm must not be assigned a universal moral, religious, class, national, or gender meaning.
The used-for and interaction labels are English-language research abstractions and do not guarantee cross-lingual sense equivalence.
Culturally specific handling or taboo should require explicit localized evidence rather than stereotype completion.
source_biases: HICO inherits web-image, common-object, human-body, and category-selection biases and omits many rare or nonphotographic interactions.
TaskGrasp emphasizes tabletop household objects, robot stability, canonical object poses, and crowdsourced task judgments.
Both sources optimize recognition or robotic manipulation rather than authorial illustration, viewer response, safety, or narrative quality.
Reported frequency, accuracy, and held-out performance must remain source diagnostics rather than runtime aesthetic weights.
runtime_implications: Store object identity separately from affordance candidates, active event role, state, resource claims, and semantic-load metrics.
Resolve hard user slots and embodiment capabilities before action-object retrieval; use creativity only after hard gates.
Jointly select action, prop, target, grasp, contact region, phase, and result rather than sampling them independently.
Keep apple, hammer, and machine gun addressable in the same global namespace while assigning different default priors and typed requirements.
Make weapon eligibility a hard typed guard external to semantic-distance ranking and authorial creativity.
Log the rejected affordance, failed predicate, occupied resource, distance debt, and required bridge for deterministic audits.
evaluation_implications: Test the same fixed concept and seed with apple, hammer, and machine gun while scoring core preservation, event coherence, resource conflicts, theme displacement, and policy separation independently.
Mutation tests must reject closed-slot insertion, impossible grip, absent instrument target, unsupported remote prop, and creativity-based weapon-policy bypass.
Pixel review must distinguish mere object presence from actor-contact-target-result evidence at native and thumbnail scales.
Holdouts should include unseen object-task pairs, human and nonhuman embodiments, one-hand and two-hand conflicts, solo and dyad transfer, and no-prop requests.
Audit candidate frequency separately from acceptance and image quality so long-tail coverage cannot masquerade as improvement.

title: Discovering States and Transformations in Image Collections
limitations: The dataset learns visual states from image collections rather than observing a controlled before-and-after event for each object instance.
State adjectives and antonym pairs do not prove causal order, responsible actor, ownership, duration, or the exact prior event.
The object, scene, and material categories are bounded and do not cover all wear, repair, weapon, fictional, or cultural states.
Cross-category generalization does not mean every learned state is physically applicable to every object.

title: Learning Human Activities and Object Affordances from RGB-D Videos
limitations: CAD-120 contains a small set of indoor daily activities, actors, objects, and RGB-D capture conditions.
Its affordance labels are task annotations for activity recognition and are not a complete ontology of material state or object history.
Video context can support temporal interpretation that a single illustration cannot reproduce directly.
The study does not establish aesthetic value, cultural universality, safety, or reliable ownership and intent inference.

research_questions: Which object states are directly visible in one image and which require a before-after, action, or history inference?
How can an event action connect current state, state change, residue, wear, and repair without inventing an exact unseen past?
How should weapon state be typed when loaded status or operational readiness is not reliably visible?
Which traces remain legible at native and thumbnail scale without turning every prop into exposition?

mechanisms.statement: Represent visible object state and state change as semantically meaningful evidence of physical or functional properties rather than as decorative adjectives.
Reuse a state concept across object classes only after checking that the target material, geometry, and function can exhibit that state.
Link object state to the surrounding subaction and activity context because the same visible object can support different interpretations across event phases.
Resolve actor action and object affordance-state together so state does not float independently of contact, target, or consequence.
Bind current state, optional prior state, selected action, and visible result as a typed transition while marking any unobserved endpoint as authored rather than measured.
Use localized wear, repair, residue, and contact patterns as bounded visual clues of repeated use or intervention without asserting one exact biography.
Separate directly visible alteration from inferred duration, owner, cause, sequence, and emotional meaning; omit unsupported history claims.
Store a weapon's authored high-level state and event relation explicitly, while treating visually ambiguous loaded status, readiness, legality, or intent as unknown and keeping policy independent.

candidate_definitions.ush_observable_prop_state: A present-tense state described only through visible shape, material, fill, openness, integrity, wetness, residue, temperature proxy, arrangement, or contact evidence.
candidate_definitions.ush_state_transition_pair: A typed prior-state to current-state or current-state to intended-result relation with explicit observed versus authored endpoint status.
candidate_definitions.ush_action_state_link: A binding from actor action and phase to the object state it requires or causes and the pixel evidence that should reveal the link.
candidate_definitions.ush_use_wear_trace: Localized polish, abrasion, deformation, staining, compression, or depletion at a plausible repeated-use contact region.
candidate_definitions.ush_repair_trace: A visible patch, stitch, replaced part, fastener, weld, reinforcement, or material mismatch that demonstrates intervention without proving who repaired it.
candidate_definitions.ush_residue_trace: A visible deposit, spill, dust path, scorch, moisture edge, fragment field, food remnant, or other consequence left by a bounded event.
candidate_definitions.ush_contact_history_trace: A repeated hand, tool, foot, strap, hinge, storage, or support-contact pattern whose location agrees with the current affordance profile.
candidate_definitions.ush_weapon_state_visibility: A high-level visible relation such as stored, cased, mounted, carried, surrendered, inspected, damaged, or active-use, with visually ambiguous loaded or ready status retained as unknown.
candidate_definitions.ush_history_inference_guard: A guard prohibiting a visible trace from proving exact owner, duration, intent, sequence, moral status, or unseen event without separate evidence.
candidate_definitions.ush_state_legibility_guard: A guard requiring the selected state or transition to have a scale-appropriate material boundary, object relation, or consequence cue rather than relying on a label alone.

pixel_evidence_definitions.ush_use_wear_trace: Wear is localized to one or more mechanically plausible contact regions and differs visibly from generic all-over grunge.
pixel_evidence_definitions.ush_repair_trace: Original and replacement materials meet at a clear patch, seam, fastener, weld, reinforcement, or alignment change without requiring text explanation.
pixel_evidence_definitions.ush_residue_trace: A residue has a legible source, path, contact boundary, or settling pattern that connects it to the selected event consequence.
pixel_evidence_definitions.ush_contact_history_trace: Repeated contact marks align with the same handle, edge, support, hinge, strap, or working region used by the current action.
pixel_evidence_definitions.ush_weapon_state_visibility: Case, mount, sling, table, hands, damage, surrender gap, or active target relation visibly establishes a high-level weapon state while ambiguous operational details remain unclaimed.

compatibility: Visible wear is compatible with a current use when both occupy mechanically plausible contact regions and the current action does not erase the trace.
Repair trace is compatible with continued use when reinforcement, replacement, and load direction agree.
Residue is compatible with aftermath, recovery, cleaning, evidence, or transformation roles when it has a readable source or path.
A stored, cased, mounted, carried, surrendered, inspected, damaged, or active weapon state is compatible only with the corresponding event role and weapon guard.
One object may show present state plus one historical trace and one immediate consequence if they remain spatially distinct and causally connected.
State transition is compatible with a still image when one endpoint is visible directly and the other is recoverable from a clear action or consequence rather than prose.
conflicts: Generic all-over distress conflicts with a claim of localized use history.
A pristine surface conflicts with a selected heavy-wear trace unless repair, replacement, protected storage, or another explicit bridge explains it.
A wet-to-dry or intact-to-broken transition conflicts with no material boundary, debris, source, action, or aftermath cue.
Exact loaded, armed, safe, legal, intentional, or threatening weapon status conflicts with pixels that do not establish it.
Multiple unrelated residues and repair systems conflict with a sparse single-event bundle when they imply separate unbridged premises.
A state candidate conflicts with a user-fixed pristine, unused, undamaged, no-residue, or closed-state request.
counterexamples: Rust can arise from environment rather than repeated use, so it is not automatically a contact-history trace.
A patch may be decorative rather than a repair unless material discontinuity and structural placement support intervention.
An open container does not prove it was just opened, and an empty container does not prove who emptied it.
A cased firearm does not reveal loaded status, ownership, legality, or intent.
An apple can be fresh, cut, bitten, bruised, cooked, preserved, or rotten; no one state is its default narrative role.
A hammer with a polished handle may be frequently used, intentionally finished, or newly manufactured; exact history remains uncertain.
boundaries: Describe visible state evidence before any authored history hypothesis.
Do not infer owner, perpetrator, victim, intent, legality, age, duration, or moral meaning from wear or residue alone.
Do not equate dirt, damage, or roughness with authenticity, poverty, villainy, neglect, or artistic quality.
Do not infer weapon readiness or loaded state from appearance when it is not directly established; policy remains separate and authoritative.
Preserve user-declared pristine, broken, repaired, empty, full, open, closed, stored, or active states as fixed.
A prompt audit can verify state wording but only rendered pixels can verify state legibility.
domain_limits: MIT States focuses image collections and CAD-120 focuses a small set of indoor activities; industrial, medical, military, ritual, magical, and extreme-environment histories need separate evidence.
The matrix supports visible state and bounded history clues in a still image, not forensic reconstruction or material certification.
Thermal, chemical, electrical, internal, loaded, sterile, toxic, or otherwise invisible states require explicit safe proxies or remain unknown.
Long-term object biography is outside the direct evidence of a single generated image.
embodiment_limits: Wear and contact traces must be mapped to the actual anatomy, tool, support, or mechanism that could create them.
Nonhuman or faceless actors can produce state change without human hands, but the alternative contact and force path must be visible.
Object weight, scale, flexibility, heat, sharpness, and support condition constrain which states and repairs are physically credible.
A character unable to reach or manipulate the affected region requires an assistant, mount, machine, magic rule, or environmental process.
cultural_limits: Repair visibility, patina valuation, cleanliness norms, ceremonial aging, inheritance, disposal, and preservation practices vary across cultures and periods.
A repaired object must not be treated universally as poor, cherished, shameful, authentic, sacred, or sustainable.
Weapon storage, display, surrender, and inspection conventions vary by jurisdiction, institution, period, and genre.
Text, insignia, or culturally specific markings are not necessary to make state evidence legible and should not be invented as stereotypes.
source_biases: MIT States derives states from curated image collections and language labels, which can overrepresent visually obvious transformations.
CAD-120's indoor RGB-D activities, small participant set, and predefined labels narrow its temporal and object coverage.
Both sources privilege human-observable external state and omit many internal or culturally interpreted conditions.
Recognition performance and category frequency do not measure prompt usefulness, pixel clarity, historical truth, or artistic quality.
runtime_implications: Store current visible state, optional prior state, transition, action cause, evidence strength, and uncertainty as separate typed fields.
Select at most one primary state transition, one use or repair history trace, and one immediate residue for a sparse event bundle.
Require every historical trace to bind to an affordance contact region, environment source, repair junction, or current consequence.
For weapons, keep high-level state, target relation, event role, and policy result separate; unknown operational details remain unknown.
Reject state candidates that violate fixed user conditions, material capability, scale visibility, or event-phase coherence.
Expose observed versus authored versus unknown endpoints in the audit trace.
evaluation_implications: Mutation tests must reject ungrounded exact history, generic grunge as use evidence, invisible state labels, weapon readiness inference, and fixed-state overwrite.
Native and thumbnail review should verify one material boundary or object relation for each selected state and consequence.
Holdouts should cover fresh versus repaired apple-related objects, hammer wear at working contacts, stored versus active high-level weapon relations, no-history requests, and nonhuman manipulators.
Compare prompt-only audit with metadata-free pixel review so state wording cannot substitute for visible evidence.
Score present-state legibility, transition causality, trace localization, history overclaim rate, and theme preservation separately.

title: FrameNet Project
limitations: FrameNet is a lexical-semantic resource based on annotated language, not a visual-event dataset or illustration composition study.
Frame elements are frame-specific and should not be flattened into one universal role inventory without preserving sense and context.
English lexical coverage does not guarantee exact cross-lingual role equivalence or culturally neutral event interpretation.
Language examples can mention invisible participants, causes, intentions, ownership, or results that a single image cannot prove.

title: Visual Genome: Connecting Language and Vision Using Crowdsourced Dense Image Annotations
limitations: Visual Genome relationships and attributes are crowdsourced descriptions of web images and contain reporting, vocabulary, and canonicalization bias.
A pairwise relation does not by itself establish event phase, causal direction, intent, ownership, or narrative importance.
Dense annotation frequency is not evidence of artistic quality, universality, or the best prompt structure.
The source emphasizes natural photographs and does not validate nonhuman anatomy, stylized illustration, fantasy physics, weapon policy, or thumbnail legibility.

research_questions: How can one prop occupy instrument, target, recipient-transfer, goal, obstacle, trigger, evidence, or ownership-related roles without treating any role as inherent to the object?
Which semantic event participants must be converted into visible object relations before a still image may claim them?
How should ownership and narrative roles remain authored hypotheses when possession, transfer, storage, or markings do not prove legal or personal ownership?
Which typed role fields make a weapon's state, target, and event participation auditable without allowing creativity to bypass policy?

mechanisms.statement: Represent an event, relation, or entity through a sense-specific frame and its participants rather than a single undifferentiated prop tag.
Assign instrument, target, recipient, result, goal, obstacle, trigger, evidence, or ownership status per event because the same object can occupy different roles.
Realize a role-bearing relation as a directed subject-predicate-object structure with visible participants and an interpretable spatial or contact relation.
Combine object identity, visible state attributes, and pairwise relations into a small scene graph instead of inferring event meaning from object presence alone.
Map each selected semantic participant to an actor, prop, target, recipient, contact, gap, orientation, or consequence that can be inspected in pixels.
Treat goal, obstacle, trigger, evidence, gift, heirloom, or clue as authored narrative roles whose visible support must be specified and whose broader story remains unproven.
Separate physical possession, control, transfer, storage, marking, and declared ownership; a single image may support the first relations without proving legal or enduring ownership.
Bind any weapon to high-level state, actor or holder, event role, target relation or explicit no-target state, consequence, bystander exposure, and platform-policy result before selection.

candidate_definitions.uer_event_participant_frame: A sense-specific event record binding actor, action, target, instrument, recipient, result, location, and optional cause without requiring every slot.
candidate_definitions.uer_actor_role: The participant that visibly initiates, controls, experiences, or undergoes the selected event as defined by the event frame rather than by screen position.
candidate_definitions.uer_target_role: The person, object, surface, location, or state toward which the selected action is directed.
candidate_definitions.uer_instrument_role: A prop used through a visible actor-to-prop-to-target or result chain rather than merely carried nearby.
candidate_definitions.uer_recipient_role: The participant or destination toward which a transfer, offer, delivery, allocation, or release is directed.
candidate_definitions.uer_result_role: The visible changed state, moved object, residue, repaired junction, opened gap, reaction, or other event consequence.
candidate_definitions.uer_goal_obstacle_role: An authored desired state or impeding participant that must have a visible action relationship and cannot be inferred solely from appearance.
candidate_definitions.uer_trigger_evidence_role: A prop or trace authored as an event trigger or clue, with a separate visible causal or evidentiary relation and bounded claim.
candidate_definitions.uer_ownership_status: A typed field separating unknown, user-declared owner, current possessor, controller, custodian, carrier, borrower, recipient, relinquishing party, and stored-for relations.
candidate_definitions.uer_role_bearing_contact: A visible contact, support, force, alignment, or controlled gap that establishes how a prop participates in the event.
candidate_definitions.uer_transfer_relation: A directed giver-prop-recipient relation with readable hand or carrier orientation, approach or release phase, and contact or intentional gap.
candidate_definitions.uer_result_trace: A visible state change or environmental trace spatially linked to the selected action and role-bearing prop.
candidate_definitions.uer_ownership_inference_guard: A guard preventing possession, clothing, proximity, marking, or storage from proving ownership unless the user declares it or the event explicitly establishes transfer.
candidate_definitions.uer_narrative_inference_guard: A guard limiting goal, obstacle, clue, gift, heirloom, guilt, status, and motive claims to the visible relations and authored premise actually supplied.
candidate_definitions.uer_weapon_role_target_guard: A hard guard requiring high-level weapon state, event role, target relation or explicit no-target state, consequence expectation, bystander exposure, and policy eligibility outside creativity scoring.

pixel_evidence_definitions.uer_role_bearing_contact: The actor, prop, target or support, and relevant contact or controlled gap are simultaneously legible with unambiguous direction.
pixel_evidence_definitions.uer_transfer_relation: Giver-side control, prop path, recipient-side readiness, and transfer phase read without captions; ownership beyond the transfer remains unclaimed.
pixel_evidence_definitions.uer_result_trace: A changed object state, residue, displacement, repair, opening, break, or environmental response is visibly downstream of the declared action.

compatibility: An apple can serve as target, carried object, offered item, gift, evidence, trigger, goal, obstacle, or result when one visible relation establishes that role.
A hammer can serve as instrument, transferred tool, evidence, obstacle, repair object, symbolic prop, or target when its contact and event graph agree.

A machine gun can serve as stored object, transported item, surrendered object, evidence, controlled guard instrument, damaged result, or policy-eligible active instrument only after weapon guards pass.
Instrument role is compatible with a secondary target and result trace when the actor-prop-target chain remains readable.
Recipient role is compatible with a deliberate open gap in anticipation or release phase and does not require completed hand contact.
Ownership status may remain unknown while possession, custody, transfer, or storage relations are still represented.
conflicts: One prop cannot be both actively relinquished and exclusively controlled by the same hand at the same instant without a transition phase that explains the relation.
Instrument role conflicts with no target, no contact or force path, and no anticipated or visible result.
Gift, heirloom, clue, evidence, or goal claims conflict with mere decorative proximity when no visible relation or user premise supports them.
Ownership claims conflict with ambiguous possession, nearby placement, generic markings, or a single transfer moment.
A weapon role conflicts with unknown state, absent target relation, unresolved bystander exposure, or failed platform policy even at high creativity.
Multiple disconnected narrative roles conflict with the exactly-one event spine and sparse universal-scene budget.
counterexamples: A character holding an apple does not prove it is food for them; it may be offered, inspected, evidence, or merely carried.
A hammer beside a broken object is not necessarily the cause unless actor, contact, timing, or result evidence establishes that relation.
A machine gun in a case may be cargo, evidence, stored equipment, or an exhibit; its presence alone does not prove active threat or ownership.
A labeled or monogrammed object may be borrowed, issued, inherited, stolen, or misidentified; markings do not establish legal ownership.
An obstacle can be cooperative equipment or a protected object rather than an enemy, and a recipient need not be a person.
boundaries: Event and narrative roles are authored scene semantics, not deductions about a real person's intent, character, guilt, relationship, or legal status.
Do not infer ownership, consent, authority, rank, culture, religion, class, or morality from possession or proximity alone.
Do not let a role label substitute for visible actor-action-target-contact-result evidence.
Weapon state, target, role, bystander, and platform-policy fields are mandatory and cannot be overridden by creativity or narrative importance.
Preserve user-fixed owner, recipient, target, no-target, no-weapon, no-contact, and no-consequence instructions.
Generated text, insignia, badges, or logos are not required as proof of event role or ownership.
domain_limits: FrameNet models language and Visual Genome models photographed scene descriptions; neither is a complete narrative theory or policy system.
Legal ownership, custody, evidence status, consent, medical use, military authority, and religious significance require domain-specific evidence beyond this matrix.
Single-frame illustration can show a decisive relation but cannot prove an extended plot, lawful title, or hidden motivation.
Highly abstract, diagrammatic, or non-object scenes may require different participant realization than object-centric graphs.
embodiment_limits: Actor, target, instrument, and recipient can be human, nonhuman, machine, environment, or collective only if available capabilities and contacts support the role.
Transfer requires compatible reach, carrier surfaces, support, scale, and timing; it must not fabricate human hands for nonhuman actors.
Instrument use requires a force and support path appropriate to object mass and embodiment.
Faceless or limbless actors may express role through orientation, mounts, mechanisms, environmental response, or assistants rather than human gaze and grip assumptions.
cultural_limits: Gift, evidence, heirloom, sacred object, status symbol, surrender, custody, and ownership conventions vary by culture, period, institution, and genre.
Do not assign universal narrative meaning to apple, hammer, firearm, color, emblem, handling gesture, or placement.
FrameNet's English lexical frames and Visual Genome's English descriptions require cross-lingual sense checks.
Culturally specific roles should be described through visible event relations and verified terminology rather than stereotype completion.
source_biases: FrameNet reflects corpus selection, English lexical senses, annotation policy, and incomplete frame coverage.
Visual Genome inherits web-image, photographer, crowdsourcing, object-category, relationship-reporting, and WordNet-mapping biases.
Both sources can encode frequently described relations more strongly than rare, nonhuman, culturally specific, or visually subtle events.
Annotation density and lexical coverage do not measure artistic quality, audience engagement, or safe policy eligibility.
runtime_implications: Create exactly one event frame with typed participant slots; allow optional roles but reject every selected atom that lacks an edge to the frame.
Store object identity, current possessor, declared owner, event role, target relation, and narrative hypothesis separately.
Require a pixel evidence phrase for every selected instrument, transfer, trigger, evidence, goal, obstacle, or result role.
Use directed relation predicates and resource claims before seed or creativity ranking.
For weapons, run state-role-target-bystander-policy guards before semantic-distance and salience ranking.
Emit an audit trace distinguishing user-declared, source-prior, design-inferred, visibly required, and unknown role fields.
evaluation_implications: Mutation tests must reject prop presence without role, instrument without target, transfer without giver-recipient direction, ungrounded ownership, orphan clue, and weapon-policy bypass.
Metadata-free pixel review must identify actor, action, prop role, target or recipient, contact or gap, and consequence at native and thumbnail scales.
Holdouts should rotate apple, hammer, and machine gun through at least three different event roles while keeping identity core fixed.
Test human, nonhuman, solo, dyad, ensemble, environmental actor, no-prop, no-target, and closed-recipient cases.
Score role correctness, directed relation legibility, ownership overclaim, narrative overclaim, orphan rate, and theme preservation separately.

title: Introducing the Open Affective Standardized Image Set (OASIS)
limitations: OASIS ratings are normative responses to complete images, not inherent scores for isolated props or guaranteed responses to generated illustrations.
The norming sample was restricted to United States MTurk workers and overrepresented some demographic groups, limiting cultural generalization.
Valence and arousal do not encode safety policy, legality, violence type, physical burden, narrative role, or visual salience.
The source images, categories, crops, and 2015 collection context do not cover every subculture genre or contemporary audience.

title: Fixations on Objects in Natural Scenes: Dissociating Importance from Salience
limitations: The experiment used a bounded set of authored photographs and manipulated luminance contrast; it does not establish a universal attention model for illustration.
Object importance was operationalized through naming frequency and is not equivalent to narrative value, artistic quality, preference, or commercial impact.
Fixations are a proxy for selective attention and do not prove emotion, comprehension, attachment, or desired viewer response.
The study does not measure physical burden, hand occupancy, violence policy, semantic distance, or prompt-generation performance.

research_questions: How can physical burden, hand occupancy, affective valence, affective arousal, violence context, visual salience, scene importance, and theme displacement remain separate load dimensions?
When does a remote prop enrich a fixed concept, and when does its scale, contrast, risk, or premise become the new theme?
How should creativity change semantic-distance eligibility without changing platform-policy eligibility or rewarding high arousal and violence?
How can an apple, hammer, and machine gun receive different default priors while any of them may become low or high load under a specific event and composition?

mechanisms.statement: Represent normative affective valence and arousal as separate viewer-response dimensions rather than one emotional intensity or goodness score.
Treat affective load as a scoped prediction or norm about a complete image and audience sample, not an inherent universal property of a prop.
Separate scene importance from visual salience because an object can attract fixation without carrying the scene's intended meaning and vice versa.
Track contrast, size, placement, isolation, and other salience carriers independently from event role and narrative importance.
Measure whether a context-incongruent or visually altered prop changes what viewers treat as characteristic of the scene rather than assuming surprise is harmless.
Combine affective response and attention evidence only as distinct axes in a load vector, never as a single novelty, universality, or quality score.
Store mass, scale, support, hand or limb occupancy, recoil or force class, and mobility burden separately from affective, violence, and visual loads.
Keep violence context and platform-policy eligibility as typed guards outside creativity; a higher creativity value cannot authorize a weapon or unsafe scene.
Permit at most one remote or high-load prop premise and require the fixed identity core to retain a separate readable anchor and causal bridge.
Keep source frequency, naming frequency, affect norms, fixation probability, quality, and creative value as different measurements with no automatic substitution.

candidate_definitions.usl_physical_burden_load: A metric for prop mass, scale, support, force, recoil or resistance class, mobility effect, and resulting pose demand relative to the selected embodiment.
candidate_definitions.usl_hand_occupancy_load: A metric for required hands, limbs, mouth, tail, tentacles, mounts, assistants, and duration of resource occupation during the selected phase.
candidate_definitions.usl_affective_valence_load: A scoped predicted positive-negative viewer-response dimension for the complete scene, stored with audience and context uncertainty rather than as an object essence.
candidate_definitions.usl_affective_arousal_load: A scoped predicted intensity or activation dimension for the complete scene, independent of whether the response is positive or negative.
candidate_definitions.usl_violence_context_load: A typed metric for weapon presence, threat relation, target, active force, injury or damage consequence, bystander exposure, and genre context; it is not policy eligibility.
candidate_definitions.usl_visual_salience_load: A metric for the prop's relative size, contrast, isolation, edge strength, centrality, motion cue, and foreground occupation.
candidate_definitions.usl_scene_importance_load: A metric for how necessary the prop is to recognizing the selected event and fixed concept, kept distinct from how much attention it attracts.
candidate_definitions.usl_theme_displacement_load: A metric for how much the prop's new role, era, technology, tone, violence, scale, or salience would replace the fixed concept as the scene's dominant premise.
candidate_definitions.usl_remote_prop_budget: A router allowing at most one remote or high-load optional prop after hard gates, with required causal bridge and identity-anchor preservation.
candidate_definitions.usl_core_identity_anchor: A visible fixed-concept feature, role action, silhouette, garment relation, or characteristic mechanism that remains readable independently of the optional prop.
candidate_definitions.usl_high_load_prop_carrier: A deliberately bounded region and event relation that contains a high-load prop without allowing it to occupy every focal, hand, action, and narrative resource.
candidate_definitions.usl_theme_hijack_guard: A guard rejecting an optional prop when its premise, scale, salience, violence, technology, or resource claims erase or contradict the fixed identity core.
candidate_definitions.usl_policy_separation_guard: A guard requiring platform-policy eligibility to pass independently of creativity, distance, affective rating, genre, rarity, narrative importance, or visual appeal.
candidate_definitions.usl_frequency_quality_guard: A guard prohibiting source count, naming frequency, fixation rate, average valence, or arousal from becoming quality, universality, desirability, or creativity scores.

pixel_evidence_definitions.usl_core_identity_anchor: At native and thumbnail scale, at least one fixed identity, role, silhouette, costume relation, or signature mechanism reads without relying on the optional prop.
pixel_evidence_definitions.usl_high_load_prop_carrier: The prop has one bounded carrier region and one event role while the core subject, action, and consequence retain separate visual territory and hierarchy.

compatibility: An apple is often low physical and violence load, but can carry high affective, symbolic, scale, or salience load depending on state, event role, and composition.
A hammer can have low violence load in repair or transfer, moderate physical and hand load, and high salience only when size, swing, impact, or framing makes it dominant.
A machine gun normally carries high violence, technology, policy, hand, and salience concerns, but its active load still depends on state, target, role, scale, placement, and context.
A remote prop is compatible with high creativity only after all hard gates and when one causal bridge returns its action and consequence to the fixed core.
High scene importance is compatible with restrained salience when the prop is a subtle but necessary causal clue.
High salience is compatible with low scene importance only when it is intentionally bounded and does not displace the promised subject or event.
conflicts: High-load prop selection conflicts with another remote premise, another foreground peak, unresolved hand or support claims, or absent core anchor.
A weapon candidate conflicts with failed policy eligibility regardless of low visual salience, benign color, stylization, or high creativity.
Theme preservation conflicts with an optional prop that changes era, occupation, genre, conflict, or power relation without a visible bridge.
Affective arousal conflicts with being used as proof of quality, viewer preference, commercial value, or safety risk by itself.
Visual salience conflicts with scene importance when the optional prop attracts attention but has no event role, consequence, or relation to the fixed concept.
Closed prop, weapon, violence, empty-hand, or low-arousal instructions conflict with candidate ranking that would insert the prohibited load.
counterexamples: A giant glowing apple can hijack a maid-character portrait more strongly than a small cased weapon in the background.
A heavy hammer used to repair a halo can be physically demanding yet low in violence context and strongly connected to identity.
A machine gun surrendered, archived, or transported can be narratively important without an active attack, but policy and weapon guards still apply.
A tiny high-contrast object can dominate attention despite low mass and low hand occupancy.
A large muted prop can occupy much of the frame yet remain low in fixation salience while still displacing theme through premise and era.
High arousal can arise from joy, awe, danger, or surprise, so arousal is neither violence nor negative valence.
boundaries: Affective ratings are scoped viewer-response norms or predictions, not universal reactions or inherent object properties.
Visual salience, scene importance, theme displacement, creative value, and artistic quality remain separate.
Platform policy is authoritative and cannot be replaced by creativity, genre framing, violence score, salience, affect, or narrative role.
Do not equate weapon presence with character morality, intent, culture, gender, maturity, or criminality.
Do not treat low frequency as originality or high frequency as quality.
User-fixed identity, action, prop, no-prop, no-weapon, tone, and violence constraints override optional surprise.
domain_limits: OASIS studies complete affective photographs and the attention experiment studies natural-scene photographs; neither directly validates generated subculture illustration.
Physical burden and hand occupancy require mechanics and embodiment evidence from other research topics; they are explicitly design-inferred here.
Weapon legality, safety, and platform policy require external authoritative rules and are not supplied by these sources.
Commercial conversion, long-term attachment, cultural reception, and historical originality remain outside the matrix.
embodiment_limits: Physical and hand loads are relative to body scale, strength, limb count, grip type, support, mobility aids, mounts, and selected action phase.
Nonhuman embodiments may lower one resource cost and raise another; human two-hand assumptions cannot be copied automatically.
Recoil, impact, balance, reach, and support cues must remain physically coherent at the chosen level of stylization without operational detail.
Faceless, limbless, collective, or environmental actors require nonfacial and nonhand core anchors.
cultural_limits: Valence, arousal, weapon response, object importance, symbolic load, and genre expectation vary across cultures, subcultures, periods, and audiences.
OASIS's United States online norming sample must not be treated as global.
Apple, hammer, and firearm symbolism must not be assigned universal religious, national, class, gender, or moral meaning.
Culturally specific readings require localized sources or explicit user framing and should remain hypotheses.
source_biases: OASIS uses a 2015 United States MTurk sample and broad but curated online images, with overrepresentation of some demographics.
The salience study uses a bounded collection of artist-composed photographs, object naming frequency, and contrast manipulation.
Both sources study viewer response to existing images rather than prompt construction, nonhuman characters, or generated illustration.
Norm means and fixation counts can obscure individual variation and must not become deterministic runtime truth.
runtime_implications: Represent load as a vector with independent physical, occupancy, affective valence, affective arousal, violence, salience, importance, and theme-displacement fields.
Run user-slot, embodiment, weapon, and platform-policy hard gates before creativity or semantic-distance ranking.
Allow at most one optional remote or high-load prop and require a complete causal bridge plus one independent core identity anchor.
Compute theme-hijack from changed premise, resource claims, event centrality, and salience displacement rather than object category alone.
Keep apple, hammer, and machine gun globally retrievable with different priors but context-sensitive final loads.
Record each load axis, source or inference status, policy result, selected bridge, and rejected alternative in the deterministic trace.
evaluation_implications: Freeze the same identity core, format, and seed while substituting apple, hammer, and machine gun across low, medium, and high creativity bands.
Score physical feasibility, hand occupancy, affective hypothesis, violence context, salience, scene importance, theme displacement, policy result, and core preservation separately.
Mutation tests must reject creativity-based policy bypass, two remote high-load props, missing core anchor, orphan salient prop, and closed-slot insertion.
Metadata-free native and thumbnail review must identify the fixed core before or alongside the high-load prop and recover the prop's event role and consequence.
Track candidate frequency and acceptance separately from quality so rare high-load selection cannot be celebrated merely as diversity.
